name: assertions-not-assignments
title: Assertions are not assignments. Step through: each assertion is added to
text:
% Assertions are not assignments. Step through: each assertion is added to
% the computation, and whatever can be done is done.
X = Y        % two unknowns: the equation is suspended on both
Y = Z        % another
Z = 42       % Z is instantiated; Y = Z is reactivated, then X = Y
A = [X, Y, Z]
X = 17       % contradicts what is known: no derivation survives

name: append
title: Elcock 1990, p. 8 and pp. 9-10: append, and the goal app([1], U, [1,2])
text:
% Elcock 1990, p. 8 and pp. 9-10: append, and the goal app([1], U, [1,2]).
app = lambda R, S, T
    {R = [], S = T} or
    {R = [X|L], T = [X|N], app(L, S, N)}

app([1], U, [1,2])
tout("U", U)

name: reverse
title: Elcock 1990, pp. 11-13: a simple example of suspended equations
text:
% Elcock 1990, pp. 11-13: a simple example of suspended equations.
rev1 = lambda R, S, T
    {R = [], S = T} or
    {R = [X|L], rev1(L, [X|S], T)}
rev = lambda R, S
    {rev1(R, [], S)}

rev([1,2,U], [V|L])
% the derivation hibernates with U = X₃ and X₃ = V suspended; now add:
rev([5], [V])

name: students
title: Elcock 1990, p. 15: the completion of Clark's student "microdatabase",
text:
% Elcock 1990, p. 15: the completion of Clark's student "microdatabase",
% rendered in Absys. Transcribed as printed, with two misprints corrected:
% the second alternative of takes has C - 'C101' for C = 'C101', and the
% body of non-maths-major applies maths-course where math-course is defined.
% (sources/notes/elcock-1990.md)
student = lambda X
    {X = 'BROWN'} or {X = 'SMITH'}
math-course = lambda C
    {C = 'C101'} or {C = 'C301'}
takes = lambda X, C
    {X = 'BROWN', C = 'C101'} or
    {X = 'SMITH', C = 'C101'} or
    {X = 'SMITH', C = 'C301'}
non-maths-major = lambda X
    {math-course(C), not(takes(X, C))}

% Brown takes C101 but not C301, so Brown is a non-maths-major in Clark's
% sense; Smith takes both, and is not.
non-maths-major('BROWN')

name: setdiff
title: Elcock 1990, p. 15: "a nice example taken from a demonstration of Absys-4
text:
% Elcock 1990, p. 15: "a nice example taken from a demonstration of Absys-4
% circa 1968, using the Absys primitive aggregation operator set".
% mem is not given in the paper; this definition is ours.
mem = lambda X, S
    {S = [X|T]} or {S = [Y|T], mem(X, T)}
setdiff = lambda S1, S2, S
    {set(X), {mem(X, S1), not(mem(X, S2))}, S}

setdiff([1,2,3,4], [2,4,6], D)

name: triples
title: Foster and Elcock 1969 (MI4): item, with a key, and the triples problem
text:
% Foster and Elcock 1969 (MI4): item, with a key, and the triples problem.
% "the result would be three distinct conjunctions of assertions with
% associated data r, s, t 1, 3, 4, 1, 1, 2 and 6, 1, 7 respectively."
item'=lambda x=>z key x
    begin x = [p'&q'] {z=p or z=item(q)} end

p1 = [1;2;5;6]   p2 = [3;7;1]   p3 = [10;2;7;4]
r'=item(p1)   s'=item(p2)   t'=item(p3)   r+s=t

name: map
title: Foster and Elcock 1969 (MI4): map, with the key that makes it terminate
text:
% Foster and Elcock 1969 (MI4): map, with the key that makes it terminate.
% "map(p,f), where p is a list and f a function, should have the effect of
% asserting f applied to each item of the list." The function small is ours.
map'=lambda p, f key p
    begin {null(p) or p = [r'&s'] f(r) map(s,f)} end
small'=lambda x begin {x = 1 or x = 2} end

map([a;b], small)

title: Elcock 1982, p. 123: "Suppose we have the Absys program
text:
% Elcock 1982, p. 123: "Suppose we have the Absys program
%   u+v = 16  and  w*u = v  and  u+10 = 12
% and suppose the list of relations is initially processed in this order."
% The binding environment at the end: u is 2, v is 14, w is 7.

u+v = 16  and  w*u = v  and  u+10 = 12

name: mem-1982
title: Elcock 1982, p. 122: list membership, with a key, in the notation of the
text:
% Elcock 1982, p. 122: list membership, with a key, in the notation of the
% 1982 paper. "The assertion mem(x,[1,2,3]) is equivalent to asserting
% << x=1 or x=2 or x=3 >>. If in addition we were now to assert
% mem(x,[2,4,6]) ... then distribution would lead to nine computational
% branches of which only one, that associated with x=2, would be
% satisfiable and hence remain active."
mem = lambda m,s key  s
      << s = [p|sl] and
         << m = p or mem(m,sl) >> >>
mem(x,[1,2,3])
mem(x,[2,4,6])

name: e01-directions
title: ABSYS-E01: one procedure, several directions. Each goal below is a
text:
% ABSYS-E01: one procedure, several directions. Each goal below is a
% separate question; run one at a time with absys repl, or see e01 in
% docs/research.md for the table.
app = lambda R, S, T
    {R = [], S = T} or
    {R = [X|L], T = [X|N], app(L, S, N)}
rev1 = lambda R, S, T
    {R = [], S = T} or
    {R = [X|L], rev1(L, [X|S], T)}
rev = lambda R, S
    {rev1(R, [], S)}

name: e02-order
title: ABSYS-E02: does the order of the assertions matter?
text:
% ABSYS-E02: does the order of the assertions matter?
% The goal is written before the procedure it applies is defined; in some
% orders, before its list is known.
app = lambda R, S, T
    {R = [], S = T} or
    {R = [X|L], T = [X|N], app(L, S, N)}
app(R, S, T)
T = [1,2]

name: e03-incremental
title: ABSYS-E03: partial computation that waits for later assertions
text:
% ABSYS-E03: partial computation that waits for later assertions.
% The goal comes first; the procedure it applies is defined after it, and
% the equations that complete it come after that.
A = [X, Y, Z]
rev(A, B)
X = Y
rev = lambda R, S
    {rev1(R, [], S)}
rev1 = lambda R, S, T
    {R = [], S = T} or
    {R = [H|L], rev1(L, [H|S], T)}
Y = Z
B = [42|C]

name: e04-left-recursion
title: ABSYS-E04: a left-recursive definition of a list of a's, asked to check a
text:
% ABSYS-E04: a left-recursive definition of a list of a's, asked to check a
% list that is already known. In Prolog, as(L) :- as(M), L = [a|M] calls
% as(M) with M unknown first, and descends for ever. In Absys the equation
% L = ['a'|M] is elaborated as soon as it arises, so M is known before
% as(M) is applied.
as = lambda L
    {as(M), L = ['a'|M]} or {L = []}
L = ['a', 'a']
as(L)

name: e09-simultaneous
title: ABSYS-E09: where data-directed elaboration stops. Elcock 1982, p. 124
text:
% ABSYS-E09: where data-directed elaboration stops. Elcock 1982, p. 124:
% "much more sophisticated aggregation and solution methods would be
% necessary to deal with a conjunction of a general set of linear equations
% in n variables". Two equations, two unknowns, each relation waiting for
% two of its three numbers: nothing can be inferred, and both hibernate.
x + y = 10
x - y = 4

name: e09-triangular
title: ABSYS-E09: the same kind of system, but triangular. Each equation, taken
text:
% ABSYS-E09: the same kind of system, but triangular. Each equation, taken
% when it can be, has one unknown left, so data-directed elaboration solves
% it in whatever order the assertions are given.
x + y + z = 12
y + z = 7
z = 3
